questions.q: In which year was Anushilan Samiti founded, and who was its primary founder in Bengal?
questions.a: Anushilan Samiti was founded in 1902 by Pramathanath Mitra in Calcutta. A wrong answer (e.g., 1905 or naming Aurobindo Ghosh as founder) reveals the student confuses the Samiti's founding with the Partition of Bengal or mistakes prominent later leaders for founders.

questions.q: Why did the Partition of Bengal (1905) act as a catalyst for the growth of revolutionary organisations like Anushilan Samiti and Abhinav Bharat?
questions.a: The Partition of Bengal was seen as a deliberate British strategy to divide Hindus and Muslims and weaken nationalist unity; the massive Swadeshi protests that followed were met with brutal repression (baton charges, arrests, press censorship), convincing many youth that constitutional methods were futile and only armed resistance could work. A wrong answer focusing only on "anger" without linking to the failure of moderate politics shows incomplete understanding of the strategic shift.

questions.q: Compare the organisational structure of Anushilan Samiti and Abhinav Bharat. How did their differences affect their operations?
questions.a: Anushilan Samiti operated through a decentralized, cell-based structure with two main branches (Dhaka and Jugantar) allowing survival after leadership arrests; Abhinav Bharat was tightly centralised around the Savarkar brothers, making it vulnerable when they were arrested. A student who says "both were similar" misses how organisational design shaped their resilience — a key analytical skill.

questions.q: Analyse the British response to revolutionary violence (1907–1910). Did repression strengthen or weaken the movement? Use specific examples.
questions.a: British repression (Alipore Bomb Case 1908, Nasik Conspiracy Case 1909, deportations to Andamans) decapitated leadership and created martyrs like Khudiram Bose, but also drove the movement underground and failed to address root causes — revolutionary activity resurfaced in the 1920s (HSRA). A one-sided answer ("repression worked" or "it failed completely") shows inability to weigh contradictory evidence.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Revolutionary terrorism failed because it lacked mass support." Defend your position with evidence from Anushilan Samiti and Abhinav Bharat.
questions.a: The statement is largely accurate: both groups recruited from educated, urban, upper-caste youth (bhadralok in Bengal, Chitpavan Brahmins in Maharashtra), used secrecy that excluded peasants/workers, and avoided building parallel governance — unlike Gandhi's later mass mobilisation. However, their sacrifice created a "culture of resistance" that inspired later movements. A student who only agrees or disagrees without nuance misses historical complexity.

questions.q: Create a timeline showing the interplay between Congress politics (Moderates vs Extremists) and revolutionary actions from 1902–1910. Highlight three turning points.
questions.a: A strong timeline includes: 1902 (Anushilan Samiti founded amid Moderate dominance), 1905 (Partition of Bengal → Extremist rise, Swadeshi, revolutionary surge), 1907 (Surat Split → Extremists ousted, revolutionaries fill vacuum), 1908 (Alipore Bomb Case → Aurobindo acquitted, Barindra deported), 1909 (Madan Lal Dhingra assassinates Curzon Wyllie in London, Nasik Conspiracy). Missing the Surat Split or treating Congress and revolutionaries as separate tracks reveals poor synthesis.
